Artificial Intelligence (AI) has recently gained rapid popularity in both research and practice. This surge is primarily driven by the increasing adoption of Large Language Models (LLM), which have unlocked new possibilities and are Authors’ Contact Information: Yinghang Ma, York University, Toronto, Canada, coppelia@cse.yorku.ca; Jiho Shin, York University, Toronto, Canada, jihoshin@yorku.ca; Leuson Da Silva, Polytechnique Montréal, Montreal, Canada, leuson-mario-pedro.da-silva@polymtl.ca; Zhen Ming (Jack) Jiang, York University, Toronto, Canada, zmjiang@cse.yorku.ca; Song Wang, York University, Toronto, Canada, wangsong@yorku.ca; Foutse Khomh, Polytechnique Montréal, Montreal, Canada, foutse.khomh@polymtl.ca; Shin Hwei Tan, Concordia University, Montreal, Canada, shinhwei.tan@concordia.ca. 2025. Manuscript submitted to ACM Manuscript submitted to ACM 1 arXiv:2509.25465v1  [cs.SE]  29 Sep 2025 2 Yinghang Ma, Jiho Shin, Leuson Da Silva, Zhen Ming (Jack) Jiang, Song Wang, Foutse Khomh, and Shin Hwei Tan poised to transform our society significantly [18, 56]. Take software engineering (SE), for example. LLMs have shown great promise and are expected to revolutionize the entire software engineering lifecycle [26, 45, 65]. Companies and SE professionals have already begun adopting LLM-powered tools to boost their productivity [ 17, 62] and enhance software quality [22, 63, 78]. The research progress (e.g., [2, 37, 75, 79]) in this area is primarily demonstrated on publicly available benchmarks (e.g., Defects4J [35], HumanEval [12] and SWE-Bench [34]). Although the use of these benchmarks facilitates cross-comparison and replication, the reported results can suffer from data contamination due to the overlap between the training and the evaluation datasets [57, 83]. Consequently, the benchmark results may not accurately reflect true model capabilities and reveal their deficiencies [52, 72].

Consequently, the benchmark results may not accurately reflect true model capabilities and reveal their deficiencies [52, 72]. However, faithfully evaluating the capabilities of LLM-powered SE solutions presents the following challenges: • The LLM side: There are over270existing SE benchmarks [ 9], with new ones continuously curated or updated based on real-world datasets [20, 44]. Although data decontamination procedures can be applied during LLM training to deliberately search for and remove benchmark datasets from the training corpus [23, 47], it remains challenging to comprehensively identify and exclude all benchmark data and their associated tasks from the pre-training datasets to ensure trustworthiness. • The benchmark side: Existing benchmarks are used not only for evaluation and cross-comparison [ 55] but also for performance tuning and debugging during research and tool development [25, 74, 75]. This dual use makes it difficult to keep benchmarks open and reusable for the community while simultaneously avoiding contamination, which is crucial for faithful evaluation. Recently, dynamic benchmarking techniques have been proposed to continuously curate fresh data [4, 20, 30, 44, 48] to minimize the overlap between the training and the evaluation datasets. However, newly curated datasets may not closely resemble the same characteristics (e.g., difficulty levels and skill sets) as the original benchmarks, making it difficult to accurately track the progression of a model’s capabilities [32]. • The LLM-powered solution side: Studies show that LLM-powered SE solutions can be brittle, even in response to small code perturbations [66, 71, 83]. Unfortunately, many evaluations assess LLM-powered solutions solely on the benchmarks as they are, often overlooking robustness, except [55], which employs basic mutation techniques (e.g., operator and literal mutations).

Since such synthetic mutations may not accurately capture the complexity of real-world bugs [15, 36], there is a need for novel evaluation methodologies that can more comprehensively and realistically assess the capabilities of a given solution. Generating new bug repair tasks with previously unseen characteristics BloomAPR

BloomAPR: A Bloom’s Taxonomy-based Framework for Assessing the Capabilities of LLM-Powered APR Solutions 3 To address the above three challenges, we argue that rather than focusing solely on the difficult task of eliminating overlap between the benchmark and the LLM’s training datasets, the research community should prioritize the development of innovative evaluation methodologies that can robustly assess LLM-powered SE solutions across diverse usage contexts. Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel evaluation framework that systematically assesses the capabilities of LLM-powered solutions by incorporating Bloom’s Taxonomy [5, 6]. As shown in Figure 1, Bloom’s Taxonomy classifies cognitive abilities into six layers of increasing complexity, ranging from lower-order thinking skills that require basic cognitive processing ( Remember, Understand, Apply) to higher-order thinking skills that require more advanced and deeper cognitive processing ( Analyze, Evaluate, Create). Originally designed for educational settings, it has been widely adopted to structure learning objectives and design assessments. Integrating Bloom’s Taxonomy into the evaluation framework enables fine-grained identification of specific competencies demonstrated by a solution and highlights areas for improvement [28, 83]. Since our framework builds upon existing static benchmarks, the evaluation results are easily trackable and comparable, thereby ensuring consistency. To demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of our framework, we developed a research prototype,BloomAPR, based on the well-knownDefects4J benchmark and evaluated it on two state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLM-powered Automated Program Repair (APR) solutions: ChatRepair [75] and CigaR [25]. For each bug in the original benchmark, our framework generates multiple variations and synthesizes new versions to ensure robust evaluation.

For each bug in the original benchmark, our framework generates multiple variations and synthesizes new versions to ensure robust evaluation. Our evaluation results show that both solutions are primarily limited to basic recall (solving53 .92%to82 .71%of issues at the Remember layer). They reach a higher plausible patch rate when dealing with the synthetic code structure (88.94%to98 .61%for Fix_+ and Fix_A at the Understand layer), and then their performance drops at the Apply layer under LLM-generated rephrasing-based renaming and hash-based renaming settings (21.66%to50 .69%), showing difficulty in handling semantic variations. They also have difficulty analyzing in similar but slightly different real-world contexts and applying the learned skills (13 .46%to41 .34%for Fix_+ and Fix_A at the Analyze layer). The discrepancy between the Analyze layer and the lower layers highlights their weakness in handling large code contexts. The contributions of this paper are: • This paper introducesBloomAPR, the first systematic framework that transforms an existing static APR benchmark into a structured, dynamic evaluation environment grounded in Bloom’s Taxonomy. Unlike existing benchmarking approaches,BloomAPRorganizes evaluation tasks into layers that diagnose different cognitive capabilities of LLM- powered APR agents. Our framework not only mitigates data-contamination and robustness issues common to static benchmarks, but also addresses consistency limitations and faithfulness concerns in current dynamic benchmarks. To our knowledge, this is the first work to transform existing static benchmarks into structured dynamic evaluations grounded in Bloom’s Taxonomy. • While we reuse existing perturbation and memorization checks where applicable (e.g., at the Remember and Apply layers), we introduce new evaluation techniques—such as controlled bug injections and synthetic bug generation across diverse project contexts at the Understand and Analyze layers.

This layered structure enables not only raw accuracy reporting but also cross-layer insights into why APR agents succeed or fail. • Prior empirical studies on the impact of data contamination in software engineering tasks (e.g., [ 57, 83]) have focused on direct LLM prompting. In contrast,BloomAPRevaluates APR agents that employ agentic workflows (reflection, test-time sampling, iterative debugging), which iteratively refine bug fixes using the compiler, testing results, and contextual cues (e.g., code snippets or test cases). Our experiments reveal that these workflows do not automatically mitigate contamination effects, highlighting new research needs in reasoning and generalization for

LLM-powered APR solutions. To our knowledge, this is the first work to systematically evaluate the effectiveness of
agentic mechanisms under contamination in a controlled setting.
• BloomAPRfurther supports extensibility, allowing the incorporation of new benchmarks (e.g., SWEBench [ 34]) and
additional evaluation scenarios (e.g., code comment injection). In addition to performance benchmarking,BloomAPR
can also be useful for debugging APR agents and tuning LLM pipelines.
• We showed that existing bug-fixing SE benchmarks (e.g.,Defects4J) fail to robustly and faithfully assess the
capabilities of LLM-powered solutions due to large discrepancies across different layers ofBloomAPR. This issue
is also prevalent in many other SE benchmarks [12, 34, 61, 72]. These findings highlight the urgent need to update
existing benchmarks using our proposed framework to support more reliable evaluations.
•To facilitate replication and further research, we shared our framework and evaluation results at [1].
Paper OrganizationThe rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents the background and reviews
prior works related to this area. Section 3 describes our methodology for transforming existing static benchmarks
into dynamic Bloom’s Taxonomy-based benchmarks. Sections 4 presents the results of our case study, and Section 5
discusses the findings and their implications. Section 6 outlines the threats to validity, and Section 7 concludes the
paper.

In this section, we discuss the background and existing research related to our work.
2.1 Automated Program Repair (APR)
APR solutions automatically identify and fix software bugs without human intervention. Traditional APR solutions often
rely on generate-and-validate approaches, where candidate patches are generated and tested against a suite of test cases
to ensure correctness [31, 46, 69, 82]. Learning-based APR techniques utilize various information sources (e.g., historical
bug-fix data) to predict potential patches, thereby improving the efficiency and accuracy of repairs [ 14, 33, 80, 81].
Large Language Model (LLM)-based APR solutions utilize LLMs’ advanced capabilities to identify and fix bugs in
software code automatically. Unlike traditional generate-and-validate approaches, LLM-powered APR solutions leverage
the extensive pre-trained knowledge of LLMs to generate potential patches directly from the context of the entire
program [3, 7, 43, 77]. Consistent with prior works [25, 73–75], we evaluated the effectiveness of APR agents using
well-known metrics like Exact Match (EM), SYntactic Equivalence (SYE), and Plausible Patches (PP).

Data contamination occurs when information from the test set is unintentionally included in the training set, leading
to inflated performance metrics and compromised model evaluation. In the context of LLMs, data contamination can
significantly affect the evaluation fairness, making it difficult to assess the model’s true capabilities accurately. Prior
studies [32, 36, 58, 60] have witnessed such influence and proposed various ways to mitigate the problem. To avoid data
contamination, Jiang et. al. constructed HumanEval-Java [32] by manually converting HumanEval Python programs to
Java and injecting bugs into the correct Java programs. Meanwhile, RepairBench [60], which includes GitBug-Java [61],
featuring recent bugs from 2023, beyond the training cut-off date of most LLMs—andDefects4J, is proposed as a
framework for the standardized evaluation of frontier APR solutions. However, due to their static nature, i.e., having a
fixed set of evaluation tasks, the problems will persist as models evolve and re-train over time [16, 59, 76].

BloomAPR: A Bloom’s Taxonomy-based Framework for Assessing the Capabilities of LLM-Powered APR Solutions 5
To assess the impact of data contamination and the ability of APRs to generalize, we not only reused some existing
approaches but also introduced novel evaluation techniques. In particular, we reused existing membership inference
techniques [10, 84] at the Remember layer to examine the overlap of the training dataset and the target benchmark.
However, this result alone does not reveal the impact of memorization on APR effectiveness. Therefore, we re-ran
and re-evaluated APR agents on the original benchmark and evaluated the results to assess their impact. The name
perturbation technique at the Apply layer is similar to [83]. However, as we want to assess the effectiveness of APR
under semantic variations, we evaluated the impact of two perturbation techniques: rephrasing-based renaming and
hash-based renaming. The controlled bug injections and synthetic bug generation across diverse project contexts at the
UnderstandandAnalyzelayers are novel and are intended to assess the APR performance under logical and context
variations, respectively.

Dynamic benchmarking has emerged as a promising approach for evaluating LLMs, mitigating the limitations of
static benchmarks that are prone to data contamination and fail to keep pace with rapidly advancing generation
capabilities [11, 39, 67]. Key features of dynamic benchmarking include: (1) adaptive evaluation, tailoring more complex
tasks as models advance over time [86, 88]; (2) mitigation of data contamination by generating novel, out-of-distribution
scenarios [13, 27]; and (3) fine-grained capability assessment that dissects specific cognitive abilities such as reasoning
and problem-solving [27, 89]. For instance, DyVal [ 88] utilizes directed acyclic graphs (DAG) to create structured
reasoning tasks with controllable complexity, while DyVal2 employs meta-probing agents inspired by psychometric
theories to transform existing problems into new challenges targeting specific cognitive skills. Similarly, DARG [86]
constructs and perturbs reasoning graphs to generate diverse test samples, enabling a more comprehensive evaluation
of LLMs’ generalization and robustness.
While dynamic benchmarking has gained traction in evaluating LLMs, it remains underexplored in APR tasks. Recent
studies have introduced dynamic benchmarking frameworks in ASE that apply semantic-preserving mutations to code
benchmarks, creating syntactically new yet semantically identical programs [ 13, 24, 54]. These approaches aim to
mitigate data contamination and better assess the robustness of code understanding and reasoning models. However,
the integration of such dynamic benchmarking methodologies for the APR task remains unexplored. To address these
challenges, we propose theBloomAPRframework, which incorporates dynamic benchmarking to robustly and reliably
evaluate LLMs for the APR task by adapting to their evolving capabilities at various cognitive layers and mitigating
data contamination.

In this section, we describe our evaluation framework,BloomAPR, which systemically assesses the capabilities of LLM-
powered APR solutions. As illustrated in Figure 1, our framework is conceptually divided into six layers, corresponding
to the Bloom’s Taxonomy:Remember,Understand,Apply,Analyze,Evaluate, andCreate.
Our framework leverages high-quality data from publicly available static bug-fixing benchmarks to facilitate cross-
comparison and performance tuning. Depending on the objectives of each layer, variations of each bug instance from
the adopted benchmarks are generated using techniques such as program transformation, data synthesis, and bug
injection. Bloom’s taxonomy is hierarchical, meaning each layer builds on and assumes the competencies of those
below it. To demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness ofBloomAPR, we developed our research prototype based on
version2 .1.0of theDefects4Jbenchmark. In our design, the Remember layer evaluates whether SUEs can retrieve or

6 Yinghang Ma, Jiho Shin, Leuson Da Silva, Zhen Ming (Jack) Jiang, Song Wang, Foutse Khomh, and Shin Hwei Tan
recognize known fixes or patterns from a bug-fixing benchmark. For each bug instance in the originalDefects4J, the
subsequent layers deliberately increase difficulty and novelty in a controlled manner:
• Logical variations: the Understand layer tests whether SUEs can grasp the underlying bug logic through simple
synthetically LLM-generated bug instances that preserve bug semantics while avoiding lexical overlap.
• Lexical variations: the Analyze layer probes brittleness by introducing surface-level synthetic variations via
behavior-preserving transformations (e.g., variable or function renaming).
• Context variations: the Apply layer further increases complexity by placing bugs into diverse real-world project
contexts with external dependencies.
In this initial prototype, we did not address the top two advanced reasoning layers: Evaluate and Create. The
Evaluate layer focuses on patch assessment and selection, which is often treated as a related but distinct research
problem (e.g., [40, 41, 87]). The Create layer targets the generation of new bug types and fixes, a capability that current
APR tools cannot yet achieve. The remainder of this section explains each layer in detail. To aid explanation, we use a
running example to illustrate how an existing bug instance fromDefects4J, is transformed across different layers.

Objective: The goal of the evaluation at theRemember layer is to check whether the LLM-powered APR solutions under evaluation (SUEs) can recall or recognize facts about the target bug-fixing benchmark (Defects4J). Approach: As existing studies show that LLMs may memorize bug benchmarks [57, 83], it is very likely that many existing bug benchmarks have already been included as part of the training datasets. Hence, at the Remember layer of BloomAPR, we only included 217 bug instances (single-function-level bugs), which are added only from version 2.1.0 of theDefects4J, and intentionally removed bugs from the previous version (v1.0.0). The APR solution under evaluation (SUE) will be executed against these 217 bug instances to check whether these solutions can retrieve known bug fixes or recognize bug-fixing patterns as a result of their training process. Evaluation Schemes: These three metrics will be tracked: • % bugs withplausible patches (PP): PPs refer to bug fixes that pass all the given tests. % of bugs with PP is an optimistic measure, as some of the plausible patches may fail on additional test cases that are not included. Hence, it provides an upper bound in terms of how well the evaluated solutions can recognize known bug-fixing patterns. • % bugs withexact matches (EM)patches: EMs refer to bug fixes that exactly match the provided oracle. While there may be multiple valid ways to fix a bug, a high percentage of EMs is a strong indicator of the SUEs’ effectiveness. For each PP and its corresponding oracle code snippets, we removed comments and whitespace, then compared the resulting string sequences directly. If they were equal, the patch was classified as an EM. • % bugs withSYntactic Equivalence (SYE)patches: SYEs refer to patches that are syntactically equivalent to the oracle code but may differ in formatting or minor syntactic details. These patches do not alter the program’s behavior and are considered valid fixes due to their structural similarity.

These patches do not alter the program’s behavior and are considered valid fixes due to their structural similarity. For each PP and its corresponding oracle code snippets, we removed comments and whitespace, then tokenized the resulting code snippets and replaced variable names with generic placeholders. If the resulting sequences of tokens were identical, the patch was classified as an SYE. Figure 2 shows an example bug instance (JacksonCore-5) from theDefects4Jbenchmark. It is a bug in a parsing function that converts a string input into a number. The code block highlighted in red indicates the buggy code, while the block highlighted in green shows the fix. This bug stems from a failure to correctly handle scientific notation. The test case (“1e0”), which represents the string form of a number in scientific notation, triggers the failure. At the

BloomAPR: A Bloom’s Taxonomy-based Framework for Assessing the Capabilities of LLM-Powered APR Solutions 7
Remember layer, we retained the originalJacksonCore-5 bug, its associated bug fix, and test cases without modification.
Figure 3 shows an example of PP/SYE/EM patches for the same JacksonCore-5 bugs. Both PPs pass the existing test
cases. However, Plausible Patch 2 is invalid, as the code block fails to deal with some invalid inputs (e.g., _, +, or
blank space), which are not considered in the current test cases.

Fig. 2.Code Snippets for the JacksonCore-5 bug adapted at different layers. All these bug variants share the same
root cause (a.k.a., failure to correctly handle scientific notation) and can be triggered by the same test case (“1e0”).
8 Yinghang Ma, Jiho Shin, Leuson Da Silva, Zhen Ming (Jack) Jiang, Song Wang, Foutse Khomh, and Shin Hwei Tan

Objective: The goal of the evaluation at theUnderstand layer is to assess whether SUEs can understand the underlying
bug logic by breaking down textually completely different code segments and identifying the known bug patterns
embedded within.
Approach: We leveraged LLMs to first analyze each bug instance fromDefects4Jand then to generate novel synthetic
bugs with corresponding test cases. These synthetic cases were created based on the LLM’s analysis of each bug (e.g.,
identifying similar error messages or the same root causes). This type of evaluation differs from the Apply layer, since
the datasets here are generated entirely by LLMs rather than injected into real-world projects. As a result, the bug
instances and their surrounding code context are textually distinct from both the originalDefects4Jprograms and the
injected real-world variants, while still capturing the same failure logic. For our prototype, we picked a different LLM,
Claude 3.5 Sonnet, as our choice of LLMs to analyze the bugs and to generate synthetic datasets. We pick Claude 3.5
Sonnet due to its high quality and also to avoid potential bias and data contamination with our case study experiments
in Section 4. We have generated two groups of synthetic datasets:
• Synthetic Bugs with the same Root Causes: For each bug instance inDefects4J, we supplied Claude with the same
bug metadata, but prompted the model to identify the root causes. Then, based on the root causes of the bug, we
prompted Claude 3.5 Sonnet again to generate five sets of buggy code, bug fixes, and their corresponding test cases.
The Understand row in Figure 2 shows an example of a synthetically generated bug with the same root cause (a.k.a.,
a number format parsing failure) as theJacksonCore-5issue.

BloomAPR: A Bloom’s Taxonomy-based Framework for Assessing the Capabilities of LLM-Powered APR Solutions 9
• Synthetic Bugs with Similar Buggy behavior: For each bug instance inDefects4J, we prompted Claude to generate
five sets of buggy code, bug fixes, and their corresponding test cases by feeding the model with this bug’s buggy
functions, fixed code snippets, and error messages. Due to space constraints, please check our replication package for
an example.
These synthetically generated bugs, along with their corresponding fixes and test cases, were manually checked and
corrected to ensure validity.
Evaluation Schemes: To systematically evaluate the effectiveness of the SUEs, we have established the following clas-
sification of the SUE behavior while fixing a particular bug instance inDefects4Junder different versions synthetically
created by Claude.
•𝐹 𝐼𝑋 0 indicates that none of the injected bugs were fixed, suggesting the SUE cannot handle this bug type.
•𝐹 𝐼𝑋 1 indicates that only one of the injected bugs was fixed, reflecting limited capability.
•𝐹 𝐼𝑋 + indicates that more than one, but not all, bugs were fixed, suggesting constrained capability.
•𝐹 𝐼𝑋 𝐴 indicates that all injected bugs were fixed, demonstrating high proficiency in handling this bug type.
This classification allows for a nuanced assessment of patch efficacy, facilitating a clearer understanding of SUE’s
scope and reliability. To calculate the percentage of bugs resolved, we only aggregated𝐹 𝐼𝑋+ and 𝐹 𝐼𝑋𝐴, which reflect
consistent performance in fixing a particular bug type, and used this sum for comparison across layers. We also employed
McNemar’s Test [49] to check the statistical significance of the results. Similar to the Remember layer, % of bugs with
PPs/SYEs/EMs will be tracked.

Objective: The goal of the evaluation at the Apply layer is to determine whether the SUEs can understand the logic of
the code and subsequently apply the right bug-fixing patterns to bugs that they have previously seen but been perturbed
with lexical variations.
Approach: Various behavior-preserving code transformations can be applied here, so that the textual context of the
code is altered while keeping the runtime behavior the same. As shown in previous studies, LLM-powered SE solutions
can be brittle even in response to small code perturbations [66, 71, 83]. We only applied the simple code transformation
actions (variable and function renaming) here to check whether SUEs even possess the basic ability to understand the
logic behind the code. Alteringvariable namesaims to check whether the SUEs understand the internal logical flow of
the code within a function, and alteringfunction namesaims to check whether the SUEs understand the function-level
dependencies. These two types of renaming schemes were applied:
(1) Rephrasing-based renaming: Depending on the context of the code, alternative function and variable names are
given. The rephrased variable/function names can be misleading or contextually different from the original
names. Hence, the SUEs must understand the bug in context and reconcile potentially tricky naming cues to fix
the bugs.
(2) Hash-based renaming: Instead of texts that can be read and parsed for meaning, renaming function/variable names
with cryptic hash values forces the SUEs to comprehend the underlying logic behind the code, as these names
are no longer meaningful and cannot provide any clues regarding the purpose or the concrete implementation of
the buggy code. This tests whether the SUEs understand the logic of the bug only through the structure and
semantics of the code.

10 Yinghang Ma, Jiho Shin, Leuson Da Silva, Zhen Ming (Jack) Jiang, Song Wang, Foutse Khomh, and Shin Hwei Tan The Apply row in Figure 2 shows an example of an injected bug from a real-world GitHub project JSON-java [42]. Similar to the original JacksonCore-5 issue, this bug also involves number parsing errors related to scientific notation and can be triggered by the same test case (“1e0”). We first used the Eclipse AST package [21] to locate which buggy function and their internal variables should be renamed. Then, to generate names for the rephrasing-based renaming scheme, we fed the buggy functions to GPT-4o and prompted the model to provide alternative function names and all the internal variables within as outputs. To generate names under the hash-based renaming scheme, we wrote scripts to calculate the SHA-256 hashes for the target function names and their internal variable names, respectively. To ensure the uniqueness of the generated hash values, we concatenated these names along with the current timestamp before calculating their hash values. Finally, we replaced these names in the original buggy functions with the generated alternative names by again parsing through the AST trees of these buggy functions. For the renamed functions, we also did another pass to ensure all the invocations of these functions from the feature code and the testing code in this project are updated. For our research prototype, we selected the same 217 bug instances fromDefects4Jv2.1.0 to apply our code transformation actions. Among these cases, we managed to rename all the internal variable names of the buggy functions. We only managed to rename function names for 183 bug instances due to inheritance and function overloading for the other 34 instances.

We only managed to rename function names for 183 bug instances due to inheritance and function overloading for the other 34 instances. Depending on the renaming schemes (hash-based renaming or rephrasing-based renaming) and the renamed entities (internal variable names only, function names only, or both), a total of six variations of theDefects4J benchmark were generated. The Apply row in Figure 2 shows an example of the rephrased version of the bug. The function name _parseIndex was renamed to parseIdx, and all internal variables were renamed accordingly. The call chain within the project was also updated to ensure successful compilation. Since the test suite does not directly invoke this function, no modifications were required for the test cases. Due to space constraints, please refer to our replication package for an example of hash-based renaming. Evaluation Schemes: Similar to the previous two layers, we tracked the % of bugs with PPs/SYEs/EMs. In addition, for each bug instance, the SUE either solves it (value of 1) or fails (value of 0). Consequently, each round of evaluation can be represented as a binary vector, indicating whether each bug was solved under a particular setup (e.g., function renaming via hash values). We employed McNemar’s test [49], a statistical method to check whether the SUE results differ statistically between the Remember and Understand layers, as well as the effectiveness of APRs under different renaming schemes.

Objective: The goal of the evaluation at the Analyze layer is to check whether SUEs cananalyze new project contexts
with different build systems while adopting learned fixing strategies, dependencies, and usage scenarios.
Approach: At the Apply layer, we kept the code context the same by performing the code transformation actions on
buggy code in the same project as the original benchmark. Here, we intended to evaluate the SUE’s performance by
checking whether it can recognize the buggy patterns and apply the corresponding fixes for bugs from completely
different project contexts. This is more challenging as, in addition to understanding the structure and the logic of the
corresponding code snippets, the SUEs also need to take the coding context (e.g., external dependencies, deployment
environment, and usage scenarios) into consideration. To ensure the freshness of our evaluation datasets, we intended
to inject new bugs, which have the same characteristics as our benchmark datasets, into real-world projects. Our steps
are listed below:

BloomAPR: A Bloom’s Taxonomy-based Framework for Assessing the Capabilities of LLM-Powered APR Solutions11 • Step 1 - Code Search: For each bug instance in the target benchmark, we searched for open source projects that contain similar code snippets as the fixed versions from the benchmark. In other words, we wanted to first search for the correct version of the code from the real-world project and then inject bugs afterwards. We leveraged Microsoft Copilot [51] as our code search engine, as it can understand both natural language and code within a broader context. The search results contain not only code snippets with the exact textual matches (a.k.a., type-1 clones) but also functions with small variations (a.k.a., type-2 or type-3 clones). Unfortunately, Copilot hallucinates sometimes by returning phantom projects or non-existent code snippets. We wrote a script to explicitly filter them and output up to five candidate code snippets for each bug instance from the original Defects4Jbenchmark. Since some bug instances do not have any matches with the real-world projects (e.g., Cli-5), and some have less than five matches (e.g., only two matches for the Cli-11 bug), we ended up with a total of261code snippets from37real-world GitHub projects. • Step 2 - Bug Injection: We used LLMs to inject bugs through few-shot prompting. For our research prototype, all of the obtained code snippets from the previous step correspond to the fixed version of the selected bug instances. We used GPT-4o to inject bugs into these code snippets by supplying the corresponding bugs and their bug fixes from theDefects4Jbug instances. • Step 3 - Test Case Generation: Similar to the previous step, for each injected bug instance, we used LLMs to generate the corresponding test cases through few-shot prompting. We then reused the existing test harness from36out of the37selected real-world GitHub projects, inserting the newly generated test cases into them.

We then reused the existing test harness from36out of the37selected real-world GitHub projects, inserting the newly generated test cases into them. The one remaining project, BitStream [70], does not have any test cases. Therefore, we must develop its test harness before injecting the newly generated tests. • Step 4 - Verification and Refinement: The resulting buggy and bug-fixed versions were compiled and tested to ensure the validity of the bug/bug-fixing pairs and the effectiveness of the generated test cases. Whenever compilation errors or test execution issues arose (e.g., the test failing to reveal the bug or still failing on the fixed version), the error messages and the current implementations were fed back to GPT-4o for further refinement. This process was repeated until no further compilation or testing issues persisted. Evaluation Schemes: Same as the Understand layer, we tracked 𝐹 𝐼𝑋0, 𝐹 𝐼𝑋1, 𝐹 𝐼𝑋+, and 𝐹 𝐼𝑋𝐴 and used only 𝐹 𝐼𝑋+ and 𝐹 𝐼𝑋𝐴 to calculate the % of bugs with PPs/EMs/SYEs. In addition, we also employed McNemar’s test to check whether the evaluation results differ statistically from the previous layers.

In the previous section, we introduced our framework,BloomAPR, for systematically assessing the capabilities of
LLM-powered APR solutions. In this section, we present our case study on evaluatingBloomAPRagainst two SOTA
LLM-powered APR solutions: ChatRepair [75] and CigaR [25]. Both approaches, instead of directly prompting LLMs,
leverage LLMs through APR agents that apply reflection and test-time sampling to iteratively generate and refine
bug fixes, guided by environmental feedback (e.g., compilation, testing) or enriched problem context (e.g., failure data,
examples). Once the APR solutions were defined, to ensure consistency and generalizability of our findings, we selected
LLMs for evaluation based on their popularity and availability, resulting in the following models: (i) GPT-3.5-turbo-

The generated code treats the input (a.k.a., “$HOME” in the test case) as a single unit without accounting for more complex input such as “echo $HOME/bin”. A human software engineer could easily spot the problem and reject this patch. We also compared the % of PPs/SYEs/EMs between the two APR solutions. We observed a higher fixing rate in CigaR’s results, which shows a higher PP rate (2.39%to10 .64%increase), a higher SYE rate (74 .07%to366 .67%increase), and a higher EM rate (83.33%to475 .00%increase), compared to ChatRepair’s result. These results indicate that, using the same LLM, CigaR’s multi-stage self-reflection architecture provides greater benefits than ChatRepair’s two-stage reflection approach. Summary: Although FM-powered SUEs can produce many patches that pass the test cases for synthetically generated bugs, the proportion of valid patches is noticeably lower than theRemember layer. This raises concerns about whether these APR solutions can truly understand code logic, diagnose problems, and produce correct fixes. Furthermore, this also highlights the importance of more automated and rigorous patch review and selection processes, since these APR solutions may generate many invalid PPs.

Our case study shows that while current LLM-powered APR solutions demonstrate some reasoning ability when
addressing synthetic bugs, they largely rely on memorized patterns to generate patches. SUEs often output the same
fixed code without considering the specific context. For instance, both 𝐶ℎ𝑎𝑡𝑅𝑒𝑝𝑎𝑖𝑟 𝐺𝑃𝑇 and 𝐶𝑖𝑔𝑎𝑅𝐺𝑃𝑇 repeatedly
produced identical fixes for theCompress-7 bug, even when function names were renamed in theApply layer. Although
both SUEs employ iterative refinement using sophisticated workflows and feedback, such as compilation and test
results, these mechanisms proved ineffective, as they continued to use the original function names. This highlights two
key limitations of current LLM-powered APR solutions: (1) insufficient understanding of code structure and syntax,
and (2) difficulty adapting to complex, real-world project contexts. Novel techniques are needed to enhance the code
comprehension and context awareness capabilities, either at the model or the agent level.

section: 5.2 Patch Assessment in the Context of FM-powered APR Solutions
text:
Since ChatRepair and CigaR only generate patches that pass the pre-existing test cases, they cannot accurately assess
the correctness of their own outputs. Moreover, our manual analysis at the Understand layer reveals that many PPs
generated by these APR solutions are in fact invalid. Unfortunately, none of the existing patch assessment and selection
works (e.g., [40, 41, 87]) have focused on patches generated from FM-based solutions, whose characteristics can differ
substantially from those of rule-based or deep-learning-based APR solutions. Further research is needed in this area in
order to ensure FM-powered APR solutions are safe for practical use.
5.3 Evaluating the Capabilities of APR Solutions beyondDefects4J, ChatRepair, and CigaR
Our research prototype was demonstrated on theDefects4Jbenchmark, but the framework applies to other APR
benchmarks as well. For instance, we executed SWE-agent [79], a popular LLM-powered agentic solution, a transformed
version of SWE-bench [34], which is a Python-based APR benchmark. Our experimental results also showed a significant

18 Yinghang Ma, Jiho Shin, Leuson Da Silva, Zhen Ming (Jack) Jiang, Song Wang, Foutse Khomh, and Shin Hwei Tan
performance drop (up to 92.61%) between theRemember and Understand layers, indicating that the limitations observed
in our case study generalize beyond CigaR and ChatRepair. We selected SWE-agent instead of the two studied SUEs
because many current LLM-powered solutions are tightly coupled with specific benchmarks, making it difficult to adapt
tools like CigaR and ChatRepair to work with SWE-bench.

For each bug in the original benchmark, our framework generates multiple variations to support robust evaluation.
New strategies can be continuously added to better assess LLM-powered APR capabilities. For example, the current
Understand layer focuses on evaluating SUEs’ ability to comprehend code structure and syntax. InBloomAPR, only
renaming schemes have been applied toDefects4Jso far. To enrich this layer, changes to code comments can also be
introduced. Our initial experiments show that adding or removing textual comments significantly impacts the SUE
performance. Similarly, code refactoring or injecting code smells can also be incorporated to alter or further complicate
the project context at theApplyand/orAnalyzelayers.
5.5 Using Bloom’s Taxonomy to Evaluate LLM-powered Software Engineering Solutions
In this paper, we emphasize the urgent need to update static benchmarks, which make up the majority of current SE
benchmarks, into dynamically evolving ones to more faithfully assess and improve the capabilities of LLM-powered
SE solutions. Instead of focusing solely on eliminating overlap with LLM training data, adapting static benchmarks
using Bloom’s Taxonomy offers a promising path for comprehensive evaluation. While our framework is demonstrated
on the APR benchmarkDefects4J, it is also applicable to many other SE use cases, such as test case generation (e.g.,
TestGenEval [29]) and vulnerability detection (e.g., Vul4J [8], Big-Vul [19]).

Internal Validity: While evaluating the capabilities of LLM-powered APR solutions, we identified two primary sources
of potential confounding factors: (1)Data Contamination: we established an upper-bound baseline by evaluating SUEs
on the originalDefects4Jbenchmark, which likely overlapped with the training datasets from the underlying LLMs
due to its long-standing public availability. We then evaluated SUEs on dynamically generated bugs that are textually
and contextually distinct but semantically similar to the original bugs. By comparing evaluation results across these bug
datasets, we measured the potential impact of data contamination. (2)Bug Characteristics: To ensure fair comparison
across differentBloomAPRlayers, all dynamically generated bugs were crafted to preserve key bug characteristics (e.g.,
root causes, bug fixing patterns, and triggering test failures). This consistency enables reliable cross-layer analysis and
interpretation of evaluation results.
External Validity:Choice of LLMs and Agents: This paper presents a framework for transforming static SE
benchmarks into dynamic benchmarks structured by Bloom’s Taxonomy. We demonstrated its effectiveness by evaluating
two state-of-the-art LLM-powered APR agents (ChatRepair and CigaR) using our prototype,BloomAPR, a Bloom’s
Taxonomy-based dynamic benchmark derived from the Java-basedDefects4Jdataset. There are many LLM-powered
APR agents (e.g., OpenHand [ 64], SWE-agent [79], and AutoCodeRover [85]) introduced recently. However, these
agents’ implementations are often tightly coupled with a specific benchmark (e.g., SWE-Bench) [38], causing difficulties
in cross-comparison with other APR agents causing difficulties in cross-comparison with other APR agents which are
designed for other benchmarks or evaluation criteria. To demonstrate the generalizability of our framework, we also
appliedBloomAPRto another benchmark (SWE-Bench) using a different APR agent (SWE-agent) and observed similar

BloomAPR: A Bloom’s Taxonomy-based Framework for Assessing the Capabilities of LLM-Powered APR Solutions19 results (Section 5.3). However, even with the current number of agents and LLMs studied, it took us over three months and cost over $14,000, despite extensive pipeline optimization and parallelization. We emphasize that our goal is not exhaustive benchmarking, but to demonstrate the generalizability ofBloomAPR. Generalizability of Empirical Findings: Since our evaluation focuses specifically on Java-based function-level bugs, the findings may not generalize to other programming languages (e.g., JavaScript or Haskell) or bug types (e.g., performance or security bugs). Additionally, results from this case study may not extend to non-LLM-powered APR solutions (e.g., rule-based systems) or LLM-powered agents operating in other SE tasks (e.g., code review or requirements analysis). Construct Validity:Evaluation MetricsOur study adopts PP, SYE, and EM as the primary evaluation metrics, consistent with prior works in this area [3, 7, 14, 31, 33, 43, 46, 69, 77, 80–82]. While these metrics help estimate patch quality, they have limitations: passing test cases does not guarantee correctness, and multiple valid fixes may exist for the same bug. Further research is needed to develop automated techniques capable of reliably assessing the correctness of patches generated by LLM-powered APR solutions. Identifier names: Variable and function names often carry semantic meaning. Prior studies [ 66, 71, 83] show that meaning variable and/or function names aid LLMs in understanding code better. Our program perturbations (rephrasing-based renaming and hash-based renaming) at the Understand layer intend to deliberately test whether agents rely on superficial identifiers versus deep reasoning about the code logic. Function name rephrasing is content-based, while variable name rephrasing is self-referential. These approaches were designed to preserve semantic meaning.

Function name rephrasing is content-based, while variable name rephrasing is self-referential. These approaches were designed to preserve semantic meaning. We manually verified that these changes did not alter the intended meaning when developing our framework. The goal here is to evaluate whether APR agents can comprehend code logic and apply correct bug-fixing patterns for familiar bugs. Bug Injections: The bugs in the Apply and Analyze layers are injected into project contexts distinct from the originalDefects4Jdataset. To objectively measure their capabilities, we selected up to five diverse project contexts for each Defects4J bug (e.g., JacksonCore-5) and injected the same bug into each of them. Hence, there is always a one-to-one correspondence between the original bugs in Defects4J to the injected bugs. We then assessed how many contexts each APR agent could successfully fix (𝐹 𝐼𝑋0/𝐹 𝐼𝑋1/𝐹 𝐼𝑋+/𝐹 𝐼𝑋𝐴) as a proxy for their mastery of that specific bug-fixing technique.

LLM-powered APR solutions have shown promising results in recent years, yet their evaluation still relies heavily on
static benchmarks such asDefects4Jand SWE-bench. These benchmarks suffer from critical limitations, including the
risk of data contamination and a lack of contextual diversity needed to robustly assess reasoning capabilities. In this
paper, we proposeBloomAPR, a novel dynamic evaluation framework grounded in Bloom’s Taxonomy, which enables
structured assessment across six levels of cognitive complexity. ApplyingBloomAPRto evaluate ChatRepair and CigaR
across multiple LLMs, we found that while these solutions perform well on synthetically generated bugs, they struggle
with realistic, context-rich scenarios. Their heavy reliance on memorized patterns results in substantial performance
drops under minor code perturbations and project context shifts.
Our study highlights key limitations of current LLM-powered APR solutions and the benchmarks used to assess
them. It calls for broader adoption of dynamic, Bloom-based evaluation methods to better understand and enhance the
robustness, generalizability, and reasoning capabilities of AI-driven software engineering tools.
